title: Retries, limits and shared caches
objective: Know what the HTTP rules and a load balancer actually promise when requests are retried, refused or cached.

sources.title: IETF RFC 9110, HTTP Semantics, section 9.2.2: Idempotent Methods
IETF RFC 6585: HTTP status code 429 Too Many Requests
NGINX docs: Using nginx as HTTP load balancer (passive health checks, max_fails, fail_timeout)

intro: Four situations from real services. Each answer comes from the standard or the official docs, not from habit.

questions.prompt: A connection drops before the reply arrives. By the HTTP standard's definition, which requests are idempotent, so repeating one has the same intended effect as sending it once?

options.text: POST and PUT
options.explanation: PUT is idempotent, but POST isn't: sending a POST twice can create two orders.

options.text: Only GET
options.explanation: GET is idempotent (it's a safe method), but so are PUT and DELETE.

options.text: PUT, DELETE and safe methods such as GET
options.explanation: Right. RFC 9110 names exactly these. POST isn't on the list, which is why payment APIs add idempotency keys.

options.text: All of them, as long as the server is written carefully
options.explanation: A careful server can make a POST safe to repeat (with an idempotency key), but the standard doesn't promise it.

questions.prompt: Your client gets 429 Too Many Requests. What should it do?

options.text: Retry at once, in a loop, until it works
options.explanation: That sends even more requests to a server that just asked for fewer.

options.text: Wait before trying again, for as long as the Retry-After header says if there is one
options.explanation: Right. 429 means too many requests in a given time. RFC 6585 says the reply MAY include Retry-After, telling the client how long to wait.

options.text: Treat it as a permanent failure and give up
options.explanation: 429 is about rate, not about the request being wrong. Waiting and retrying later is expected.

options.text: Send the same request to a different URL
options.explanation: The limit is usually per client or per key, not per URL, and dodging it doesn't fix the cause.

questions.prompt: nginx balances across three servers with its built-in (passive) health checks. One server dies. How does nginx find out?

options.text: It sends a test request to every server each second
options.explanation: That's an active health check. The nginx docs list it as part of the paid NGINX Plus; the built-in checks are passive.

options.text: The dying server tells nginx before it stops
options.explanation: A crashed server can't say anything. nginx learns from the requests it sends.

options.text: It doesn't: requests keep going to the dead server until someone edits the config
options.explanation: The built-in checks do catch it, from the failing requests themselves.

options.text: A real request to it fails, and nginx avoids that server for a while (fail_timeout), then tries it again
options.explanation: Right. These checks are “in-band”: by default one failed attempt (max_fails = 1) marks the server failed. That first request still fails, so retries matter.

questions.prompt: The “My account” page shows the user's name and address. A CDN sits in front of it. Which header should the page send?

options.text: Cache-Control: private
options.explanation: Right. private means only the user's own browser may store it, never a shared cache like a CDN. MDN warns that without it, one user's personal page can be served to others.

options.text: Cache-Control: public
options.explanation: public lets shared caches store it, so one user's details could be served to the next visitor.

options.text: Cache-Control: s-maxage=600
options.explanation: s-maxage is for shared caches: it would tell the CDN to keep the page for 10 minutes, the opposite of what you want.

options.text: Nothing: a CDN can tell personal pages apart by itself
options.explanation: It can't read your intent. MDN says a personalised response without private can be stored in a shared cache and reused for other users.

title: The price that won't change
objective: Find why a cache keeps serving old data after an update, and fix it the way the cache-aside pattern says.

sources.title: Microsoft Azure Architecture Center: Cache-Aside pattern (update the data store, then invalidate the cached item)

simplifies: Dicts stand in for the database and the cache, in one program with one user. With many servers and users there are more ways to go stale; Azure's page explains why the order (database first, then remove the cached copy) matters there.
symptom: The shop raised the price of tea from 10 to 12. The database says 12, but customers who had already looked at tea still see 10, hours later.
lineWhy: update_price changes the database and stops there. The copy of the old price stays in the cache, and get_price trusts the cache first, so it never looks at the new value.

predict.prompt: db = {'tea': 10}. Call get_price('tea'), then update_price('tea', 12), then get_price('tea'). What do the two get_price calls return, as a list?

options.explanation: That's what should happen. But the first call put 10 in the cache, and nothing removed it.
The first call runs before the update, when the database still says 10.
Right. The first call caches 10. The update only changes db, so the second call finds 'tea' in the cache and returns the old 10.

options.text: A KeyError on the second call
options.explanation: 'tea' is in both the cache and the database, so nothing is missing.

options.text: Give every cached price an expiry of one hour
options.explanation: Better than never, but customers can still see the old price for up to an hour.

options.text: After db[item] = price, add cache.pop(item, None)
options.explanation: Right. Update the database, then remove the cached copy, as the cache-aside pattern says. The next get_price misses and loads 12.

options.text: In get_price, read the cache twice to be sure
options.explanation: Both reads return the same old 10. The cache was never told about the change.

options.text: Write the price to the database twice
options.explanation: The database already has 12. The stale copy is in the cache.

title: My new name disappeared
objective: Recognise replication lag behind a “my change vanished” bug, and route the user's own reads so they always see their writes.

sources.title: PostgreSQL documentation: Log-Shipping Standby Servers (streaming replication is asynchronous by default)
Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications (O'Reilly, 2017): replication lag, reading your own writes

simplifies: The lag is a fixed number of seconds here. Real lag varies, and grows when the database is busy, which is why waiting a fixed time isn't a fix.
symptom: A user changes their name from 'A. Rao' to 'Asha Rao' and taps Save. The page reloads showing 'A. Rao'. They refresh a few seconds later and the new name is there.
lineWhy: Writes go to the primary, but this read goes to a replica, which gets changes a little later (asynchronous replication). Read straight after saving, and the replica hasn't caught up yet.

predict.prompt: The replica is 2 seconds behind. The page reloads 0.5 s after the save. What does show_profile(7) return?

options.text: 'Asha Rao'
options.explanation: That's on the primary, but the read goes to the replica, which won't have it for another 1.5 s.

options.text: 'A. Rao'
options.explanation: Right. 0.5 s is less than the 2 s lag, so the replica still has the old name.

options.text: None, because the write is half-copied
options.explanation: A replica applies each change whole; it has either the old value or the new one.

options.text: An error, because the two copies disagree
options.explanation: Nothing checks the copies against each other. The replica just answers with what it has.

options.text: Sleep 2 seconds in save_profile before returning
options.explanation: Lag isn't a fixed number, so sometimes 2 s isn't enough, and every save now feels slow.

options.text: Add another replica
options.explanation: More replicas share the reads, but each one is still behind the primary.

options.text: Read the user's own profile from the primary (at least for a while after they change it)
options.explanation: Right. This is “read your own writes”: the person who just changed something reads from the copy that surely has it. Other people's profiles can still come from replicas.

options.text: Retry show_profile until the name changes
options.explanation: The reader can't know a change is coming, and if the save had failed, this would loop forever.

title: Cache a busy product page
objective: Break “add a cache” into decisions (what, which key, when to remove it), and find the cases that still hurt.

sources.title: Microsoft Azure Architecture Center: Cache-Aside pattern (lifetime of cached data; update the data store before removing the item)
MDN: Cache-Control (private: personalised responses in a shared cache can leak to other users)

simplifies: One cache in front of one database. Real systems may have several cache layers (browser, CDN, an in-memory store), each with its own rules.
problem: A shop's product pages are read far more often than products change, and the database is struggling. Plan a cache for product data that cuts database reads without showing wrong prices or one shopper's data to another.

steps.prompt: In your own words: what must get better, and what must not get worse?
hints: Better: the database load.
Not worse: correctness (prices) and privacy (one shopper's cart).
steps.model: Goal: most product reads are answered without the database. Limits: a price change shows up quickly, and nothing personal (cart, name) is ever served to another shopper.

options.text: Make every page as fast as possible, whatever it shows
options.explanation: Speed with wrong prices or someone else's cart isn't acceptable.

options.text: Answer most product reads from a cache, keep prices fresh enough, and never share personal data
options.explanation: Right. Three parts: load, freshness, privacy. Each turns into a decision later.

options.text: Replace the database with the cache
options.explanation: A cache holds copies. The database stays the source of truth.

options.text: Cache whole pages, including the shopper's cart
options.explanation: That's the privacy problem the job must avoid.

steps.prompt: Shrink it: one product, one cache, one database. What happens on the first read, and on the second?
hints: The first read finds nothing in the cache.
Whatever the first read fetched, it can leave behind for the second.
steps.model: First read: a miss, so read the database, store the result in the cache, return it. Second read: a hit, answered from the cache with no database work. That's cache-aside.

check.prompt: A read finds nothing in the cache. What happens next?

options.text: Return “not found” to the shopper
options.explanation: A miss only means the cache doesn't have it yet. The database still does.

options.text: Wait until something else fills the cache
options.explanation: In cache-aside nothing else fills it: the reader does.

options.text: Read from the database, store a copy in the cache, then return it
options.explanation: Right. The next read for the same product is then a hit.

options.text: Copy the whole database into the cache
options.explanation: Far more than needed, and most of it would never be read.

steps.prompt: List the decisions in the order you'd make them. What goes in the cache, under what key, and what happens on reads and on updates?
hints: Decide what is shared (product data) and what is personal (cart) first.
The update rule needs the key, so the key comes before it.
steps.model: Cache only shared product data, never the cart or the shopper's name; key it by product id; on a read, try the cache, and on a miss load from the database and store it with an expiry; on an update, write the database first, then remove the cached copy.

parts: Decide what may be cached: shared product data only, nothing personal
Choose the key: one entry per product id
On a read: try the cache; on a miss, load from the database and store it with an expiry
On an update: write the database, then remove that product's cached copy
check.explain: What you cache decides whether it's safe to share; the key must exist before reads and updates can use it; reads fill the cache, and updates clean up after them.

steps.prompt: An admin changes a price. In which order should the code write the database and remove the cached copy? Think about a shopper reading in between.
hints: Try “remove first”: a shopper reads between the two steps. What do they load into the cache?
The database still has the old price at that moment.
steps.model: Write the database first, then remove the cached copy. If you remove it first, a read in the gap misses, loads the old price from the database and caches it again, so the stale price survives the update.

check.prompt: Which order does Azure's cache-aside guidance give?

options.text: Remove the cached copy, then write the database
options.explanation: In the gap, a read misses, fetches the old price and caches it again. Azure warns about exactly this.

options.text: Write the database, then remove the cached copy
options.explanation: Right. “Update the data store before removing the item from the cache.”

options.text: Write the new price into the cache only; the database can catch up later
options.explanation: Then the database, the source of truth, is out of date, and a cache restart loses the change.

options.text: Either order: they happen so close together it can't matter
options.explanation: With many shoppers, something will land in the gap. The order decides what it sees.

steps.prompt: Your plan works for a normal read. Which situations still cause trouble?
hints: Think of a very popular entry at the moment it expires.
Think of what's inside a cached response, not just its key.
steps.model: Three still hurt: a hugely popular entry expiring (many requests miss at once and all hit the database, a stampede); caching a response that contains one shopper's data (it can be served to others); an update path that forgets to remove the copy (stale price). A first-ever read is just one miss, and repeat reads are the point of the cache.

check.prompt: Tap every situation that still causes trouble.

cases.text: The most popular product's entry expires during a sale
cases.why: Many requests miss at the same moment and all ask the database: a cache stampede. Fixes include letting only one request reload it.

cases.text: The cached response includes the shopper's name and cart
cases.why: The next shopper can be served that same response. Personal data must stay out of shared caches (MDN on Cache-Control: private).

cases.text: A bulk price import writes the database but skips the cache step
cases.why: Every update path has to remove the cached copy, or old prices stay until they expire.

cases.text: A product nobody has viewed before is opened
cases.why: One miss, one database read, then it's cached. That's normal.

cases.text: The same shopper opens the same product twice
cases.why: The second read is a hit. That's what the cache is for.

steps.prompt: Write the whole plan in plain words, then compare. What would you watch to know it works?
hints: Name a number that shows the cache is helping.
steps.model: Cache shared product data under its product id with an expiry, using cache-aside: read from the cache, load and store on a miss. On every update path, write the database, then remove the copy. Keep personal parts (cart, name) out of it and mark personal responses Cache-Control: private. Protect the hottest entries from stampedes, for example by letting one request reload while others wait. Watch the hit rate and the database load: if the hit rate is low, the expiry may be too short or the cache too small.

title: Charged twice
objective: See how a retry after a lost reply repeats a payment, and how an idempotency key makes retrying safe.

sources.title: Stripe: Designing robust and predictable APIs with idempotency
IETF RFC 9110, HTTP Semantics, section 9.2.2: Idempotent Methods

simplifies: The payment server always succeeds; only its replies get lost, and the client retries at once. Real clients wait longer between tries (backoff), and a real server keeps keys for a limited time.
symptom: On a day with a slow network, several customers were charged twice for one order. The logs show one timeout before each double charge.
lineWhy: A timeout doesn't mean the charge failed: the server may have charged and the reply got lost. Each retry is a brand-new charge, because nothing tells the server it's the same payment.

predict.prompt: The server charges every time it's asked. The first reply is lost (a timeout), the second arrives. What happens?

options.text: charged 1 time
options.explanation: That's what the customer expects, but the first attempt did charge; only its reply was lost.

options.text: charged 2 times
options.explanation: Right. Attempt 1 charges, the reply is lost; attempt 2 charges again and its reply arrives.

options.text: charged 3 times
options.explanation: The loop returns as soon as a reply arrives, on attempt 2.

options.text: charged 0 times, then PaymentFailed
options.explanation: A timeout only means no reply came. The server did the work.

options.text: Make a new random idempotency key for each attempt
options.explanation: Every attempt then looks like a different payment to the server, so it still charges each time. The key must stay the same across retries.

options.text: Retry only twice instead of three times
options.explanation: One lost reply still gives two charges.

options.text: Don't retry: raise PaymentFailed on the first timeout
options.explanation: The customer may already be charged yet sees “failed”, and will probably pay again by hand.

options.text: Send one idempotency key per order (for example the order id) with every attempt
options.explanation: Right. The server sees the same key, charges once, and replies to retries with the first result. Stripe's API works this way.

title: One limit, four servers
objective: Design a per-user rate limit that holds across several servers, and find where a fixed window and a non-atomic counter leak.

sources.title: IETF RFC 6585: HTTP status code 429 Too Many Requests (MAY include Retry-After)
Redis documentation: INCR (atomic increment; the rate limiter pattern)
Claude Platform docs: Rate limits (an example of a real API that uses the token bucket algorithm)

simplifies: Uses a fixed one-minute window and assumes the shared store is always reachable. Real designs also decide what happens when it isn't (allow requests, or refuse them), and many use a token bucket or sliding window instead.
problem: An API runs on 4 servers behind a load balancer. Each user may make at most 100 requests per minute in total. Over the limit, they get 429 Too Many Requests. Design the limiter.

steps.prompt: In your own words: what is counted, over what period, across which servers, and what happens over the limit?
hints: “In total” is the key phrase.
Who is the limit per: a server, or a user?
steps.model: Count each user's requests over one minute, added up across all 4 servers. The 101st request in that minute gets 429, ideally with Retry-After saying when to try again.

options.text: Each server allows each user 100 requests per minute
options.explanation: With 4 servers that allows up to 400 per user, not 100 in total.

options.text: Each server allows 100 requests per minute from all users together
options.explanation: That limits the server, not each user. One busy user could use it all up.

options.text: Each user gets 100 requests per minute, counted across all servers; extra ones get 429
options.explanation: Right. Per user, all servers combined, refused with 429.

options.text: Each user may send one request every 0.6 seconds
options.explanation: That's a stricter, smoother rule. The problem allows bursts within the 100.

steps.prompt: Shrink it: one server, one user, a counter that resets each minute. Walk through a busy minute.
hints: Count each request as it arrives.
Compare the count with 100 before handling the request.
steps.model: Keep a count for the current minute. Each request adds 1; if the count is now above 100, reply 429; at the next minute the count starts again at 0.

check.prompt: One server. The user's count for this minute is already 100, and request 101 arrives 40 seconds in. What happens?

options.text: It's handled, because the minute isn't over
options.explanation: The limit is 100 within the minute, and this would be the 101st.

options.text: It gets 429; the count starts again at the next minute
options.explanation: Right. Over the limit means refused until the window resets.

options.text: The count resets to 0 and the request is handled
options.explanation: Resetting on overflow would make the limit meaningless.

options.text: The user is blocked for the rest of the day
options.explanation: The limit is per minute. Next minute, they can send again.

steps.prompt: Every server has to check the user’s count before handling a request. List the steps one server takes, in order. Where does the count live?
hints: You need to know who the user is before you can find their counter.
Increment and read the new value in one atomic step, so two servers can't both see 99.
steps.model: Identify the user; build the key for this user and this minute; atomically increment it in the shared store (Redis INCR returns the new value) and let the key expire after the minute; if the new value is over 100, reply 429 with Retry-After; otherwise handle the request.

parts: Identify the user (for example from their API key)
Build the counter key: this user and this minute
Atomically add 1 in the shared store and read the new count
Over 100: reply 429 with Retry-After; otherwise handle the request
check.explain: The key needs the user; the count needs the key; the decision needs the count. Adding and reading in one atomic step is what keeps two servers from both seeing 99.

steps.prompt: Why must the count live in a shared store? Try the quick version: a counter in each server’s memory, limit 100 each. In the worst case, how many requests can one user get through in a minute?
hints: The load balancer spreads requests across the servers.
Each server only knows its own count.
steps.model: Up to 400: each server lets through 100 before refusing, and none knows about the others. The count must live in one place all servers share, such as a Redis key per user per minute.

check.prompt: 4 servers, each with its own in-memory counter and a limit of 100. Worst case per user per minute?

options.explanation: Only if every request lands on the same server. The balancer spreads them out.
Nothing divides the limit. Each server allows the full 100.
Right. Each server allows 100 and can't see the others' counts. Hence a shared counter.

options.text: Unlimited
options.explanation: Each server still stops at 100, so the total stops at 4 × 100.

steps.prompt: The intent is “no more than 100 requests in any 60 seconds”. Which cases break it?
hints: Look at the moment one window ends and the next begins.
What if two servers read the count, then each write count + 1?
steps.model: Two leaks. Window edges: 100 requests at 0:59 and 100 more at 1:00 are 200 within two seconds, all allowed, because each lands in a different window (a token bucket or a sliding window avoids this). Read-then-write: two servers both read 99 and both write 100, letting 101 through; an atomic increment avoids it. Steady traffic and a single burst inside one window are handled correctly.

check.prompt: Shared fixed-window counter, limit 100 per minute. Tap every case that breaks “no more than 100 in any 60 seconds”.

cases.why: Different windows, so all 200 pass within about two seconds. That's the fixed window's weak spot.

cases.text: Two servers each read the count (99), add 1 and write back 100
cases.why: Both requests pass, so 101 get through, and the count says 100. Hence an atomic increment like Redis INCR.

cases.text: 50 requests spread evenly across one minute
cases.why: Well under the limit, nothing to refuse.

cases.text: 101 requests in the middle of one minute, with an atomic counter

steps.prompt: Put the design together in plain words, then compare. What would you choose if bursts at window edges matter?
hints: Name the store, the key and the operation.
Think of the rate-limiting lesson's token bucket.
steps.model: Every server, for every request: identify the user, atomically increment a shared counter keyed by user and minute (for example Redis INCR with an expiry), and reply 429 with Retry-After when the count passes 100. Counting in one shared place makes the limit total, not per server; the atomic increment stops two servers counting the same slot. If bursts at the window edge matter, use a token bucket (the Claude API, for example, says it uses one) or a sliding window. Also decide in advance what happens if the shared store is down.
